title: Six Months In, US Immigrant Visa Freeze for 75 Countries Shows No Sign of Lifting
excerpt: The Trump administration's indefinite suspension of immigrant visa processing for nationals of 75 countries remains in effect more than six months after it was announced, with no timeline for resumption.
body:
• The US State Department suspended immigrant visa processing for nationals of 75 countries effective January 21, 2026, citing "public charge" concerns — the freeze remains indefinite with no announced end date.
  • The suspension affects permanent residency pathways including family-based and employment-based immigrant visas, but does not apply to non-immigrant visas such as H-1B, F-1 student, tourist, or other temporary categories.
  • South Asian countries Pakistan and Bangladesh are on the list; India is not, but the policy signals a broader restrictive shift that affects Indian nationals waiting in employment-based green card queues.
  • Affected applicants can still attend consular interviews, but visa issuance decisions have been halted pending a departmental review of screening criteria.

The Freeze That Hasn't Thawed

On January 14, 2026, the US Department of State announced it would pause immigrant visa processing for citizens of 75 countries. The suspension took effect on January 21. More than six months later, it remains in place.

The State Department cable that outlined the move, reviewed by Reuters, stated that nationals from the listed countries were "at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States." The department said it was undergoing a "full review" of all policies, regulations, and guidance to ensure "the highest level of screening and vetting" for visa applicants.

The 75 countries span Latin America, the Caribbean, South Asia, the Balkans, the Middle East, and much of Africa. The list includes Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Bhutan from South Asia, as well as nations like Brazil, Nigeria, Egypt, Iran, and Iraq. India is not on the list.

What the Suspension Covers — and What It Doesn't

The pause applies exclusively to immigrant visas — the pathways that lead to lawful permanent residence, commonly known as green cards. This includes both family-based and employment-based immigrant petitions processed at US embassies and consulates abroad.

Non-immigrant visa categories remain unaffected. F-1 student visas, J-1 exchange scholar visas, H-1B and other employment-based temporary visas, and B1/B2 tourist and business visas continue to be processed. Individuals who held valid visas as of January 21, 2026, are also exempt.

"Applicants from these countries are at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States."

— US State Department cable, reviewed by Reuters

Affected applicants may still attend consular interviews, according to the State Department, but their eligibility for visa issuance remains uncertain. The suspension is indefinite, with the department using the window to review "public charge" screening procedures.

The Broader Immigration Landscape

The visa freeze is one component of the Trump administration's intensifying crackdown on legal immigration. It followed a November 2025 directive to US diplomats asking them to ensure that visa applicants are financially self-sufficient. In September 2025, the administration imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications — a fee subsequently blocked by a federal appeals court in July 2026. The administration has also signaled interest in attaching a $100,000 fee to the Optional Practical Training program for international students.

The move did not impact US visitor visas, which have been in the spotlight given that the United States is hosting the 2026 FIFA World Cup and the 2028 Olympics.

Impact on the Indian Diaspora

While India is absent from the 75-country list, the policy has direct implications for the broader Indian diaspora. Pakistani and Bangladeshi nationals — many with deep cultural and family ties to the Indian subcontinent — face frozen green card applications. Nepalese and Bhutanese nationals are similarly affected.

For Indian nationals, the suspension adds to an already difficult immigration environment. The EB-2 green card queue for India stretches back more than a decade, and the combination of the proposed $100,000 H-1B fee, potential OPT restrictions, and the broader climate of policy uncertainty has prompted many Indian professionals to consider alternative immigration destinations.

"The suspension applies to immigrant visas: permanent residence pathways such as family-based and employment-based immigrant petitions."

— University of Pennsylvania, Penn Global advisory

No End in Sight

Immigration attorneys and university offices that initially expected a weeks-long review have adjusted their outlook. Yale University's Office of International Students and Scholars noted in its advisory that the pause will remain in effect "until DoS reassesses its procedures for determining whether immigrant visa applicants from these countries are likely to become financially dependent on the US government."

No timeline for that reassessment has been announced. For thousands of families with pending immigrant visa applications across 75 countries, the wait continues.
nri_angle: While India is not on the 75-country list, South Asian neighbors Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Bhutan are affected, and the policy adds to a broader restrictive shift impacting Indian professionals' green card prospects.
author: Diaspora Desk
